title: Unified memory, residency and migration
theory: unified virtual addressing versus managed allocation, residency, migration, first touch, prefetch and oversubscription. Distinguish discrete GPU behavior from coherent systems and platform-specific restrictions.
evidence: correctness and a report tied to actual memory capabilities and observed movement.
outcome: Report unified memory behavior tied to queried device capabilities and observed page migration.

key_terms.Managed memory: An allocation from `cudaMallocManaged` that both host and device can address through one pointer.
key_terms.Page migration: Moving memory pages between host and device on demand, which costs time the first time each page is touched.
key_terms.Prefetch: A `cudaMemPrefetchAsync` hint that moves pages to a processor before they are needed.
key_terms.Unified virtual addressing: One virtual address space shared by host and devices so a pointer value identifies its memory.

mistake: one pointer means one physically uniform memory pool or that managed allocation eliminates data-movement cost. .
mechanism: Unified virtual addressing concerns address-space organization; managed memory provides an allocation model whose residency and migration are managed under supported platform rules. Neither term promises uniform access cost. First touch can trigger movement, alternating host/device access can cause repeated migration, and prefetch is a placement hint with its own ordering requirements. Coherent systems, discrete GPUs and WSL can have different capabilities. Query support and use the selected platform's documented contract. A single pointer does not erase the need to reason about which processor owns useful work at each phase.
example1: A 64 MiB managed array is initialized by the CPU and then processed repeatedly on a GPU. The first GPU pass may include migration costs that later resident passes do not. Report the first pass separately rather than using a warm result to promise cold-start latency.
example2: Alternating a full CPU pass and full GPU pass for ten rounds can move the working set repeatedly. A simplified model counts twenty ownership transitions, unlike a batched design with one transfer to each side. Actual migration can occur at finer granularity and depends on platform support.

mib, transitions = 64, 20
modeled_moved_mib = mib * transitions
assert modeled_moved_mib == 1280
print({"simplified_transition_volume_MiB": modeled_moved_mib, "actual_migration_measured": False})

title: CUDA Graphs for repeated workflows
theory: define, instantiate and replay a dependency graph; stream capture, lifetime of referenced resources, launch overhead and update constraints. Explain the difference from a framework's autograd graph.
evidence: correct replay, safe resource lifetimes, a scoped comparison and explicit unsupported changes.
outcome: Capture and replay a CUDA Graph correctly and compare its submission cost against ordinary stream launches.

key_terms.CUDA Graph: A recorded set of kernels, copies and dependencies that can be launched as one unit.
key_terms.Stream capture: Recording work submitted to a stream into a graph instead of executing it.
key_terms.Graph instantiation: Turning a graph into an executable form once so later launches avoid most per-operation overhead.
key_terms.Graph update: Changing parameters of an executable graph without rebuilding it, when the topology stays the same.

mistake: a graph automatically fuses kernels or accepts arbitrary dynamic control flow without further design. .
mechanism: A CUDA Graph represents a dependency graph that can be instantiated and replayed. It can reduce repeated host submission overhead for suitable workflows, but graph creation and instantiation cost time. Resources referenced by nodes must remain valid across execution, and updates must obey the selected graph API's rules. Stream capture records supported operations in a defined capture context; it is not permission to capture arbitrary host control flow. A CUDA Graph differs from an autograd graph: one schedules execution dependencies, while the other tracks differentiation relationships. Graph replay does not automatically fuse kernels.
example1: A synthetic pipeline spends 20 microseconds submitting each ordinary iteration. Graph replay reduces this to 5 microseconds, but setup costs 300 microseconds. Ignoring other equal costs, break-even is more than twenty repeats. At exactly twenty, the submission savings merely repay setup.
example2: A graph contains fill, affine transform and download nodes with dependencies. Replay uses the same valid storage but new input contents. Changing the input shape beyond allocation capacity is not just a new value; rebuild or perform a supported update after validating all node contracts.

setup_us, ordinary_us, replay_us = 300, 20, 5
break_even = setup_us / (ordinary_us - replay_us)
assert break_even == 20
assert setup_us + 21 * replay_us < 21 * ordinary_us
print({"synthetic_break_even_replays": break_even})

title: Second capstone: a streaming numerical service core
theory: bounded queues, backpressure, chunk ownership, latency versus throughput, batching and cancellation. This is a compute pipeline exercise, not permission to open an arbitrary web server in a worker.
evidence: all outputs match, no chunk is dropped or reused early, memory stays within the budget, and the report separates request latency from throughput.
outcome: Build a bounded streaming compute core that keeps memory within budget and reports latency separately from throughput.

key_terms.Backpressure: Refusing or delaying new requests when all buffers are busy, so memory use stays bounded.
key_terms.Slot state machine: A fixed set of buffer slots, each moving through explicit states such as free, uploading, computing and draining.
key_terms.Request latency: The time from accepting one request until its result is returned.
key_terms.Memory budget: The declared maximum device and pinned host memory the service may hold at once.

mistake: maximizing batch size automatically gives the best user experience.
mechanism: A streaming compute service needs bounded ownership and backpressure before it needs more streams. Backpressure means producers stop or reject work when the system cannot safely accept another item. A slot moves through states such as free, filling, computing, copying and consumed. Reuse is allowed only after the final consumer completes. Cancellation stops admission and cleans up according to actual completion state; it does not magically cancel every submitted device instruction. This capstone is a bounded local pipeline, not a new network server inside the classroom worker.
example1: With capacity two, submit chunks A and B. Chunk C waits until a slot becomes free. If A finishes compute but its output is still downloading, A's slot is not yet free. A correct queue can process arbitrary many chunks with constant bounded storage by reusing only completed slots.
example2: A synchronous pipeline has 7 ms latency per chunk. A pipelined version can deliver later chunks every 3 ms while the first still takes roughly 7 ms in the ideal model. Throughput and first-result latency are distinct objectives; reporting only the inter-result interval hides the user's wait.

states = ["free", "filling", "computing", "copying", "consumed", "free"]
assert states.index("computing") < states.index("consumed")
chunks = [[1, 2], [3], [], [4, 5]]
results = [[2 * x for x in chunk] for chunk in chunks]
assert results == [[2, 4], [6], [], [8, 10]]
print({"reference_results": results, "slot_lifecycle": states})

title: CCCL, Thrust and CUB before writing everything by hand

evidence: equivalent semantics, stated temporary-memory needs and a justified library/custom decision.
outcome: Compare a Thrust or CUB primitive against a handwritten kernel and justify the library or custom choice.

key_terms.CUB: A CUDA library of block-level, warp-level and device-wide primitives with explicit temporary storage.
key_terms.Temporary storage query: A first CUB call with a null workspace pointer that returns the number of bytes the algorithm needs.

key_terms.Monte Carlo estimate: An average over random samples whose standard error typically shrinks in proportion to one over the square root of the sample count.

title: Softmax and reductions for model workloads
theory: numerically stable softmax, max subtraction, row reductions, normalization and shape-dependent strategies. Derive the stability improvement, then identify memory traffic and reduction dependencies.
evidence: finite outputs, row sums within justified tolerance and comparison with the CPU reference.
outcome: Implement a numerically stable row softmax and verify finite outputs and row sums against the CPU reference.

key_terms.Logit: An unnormalized score that softmax converts into a probability.
key_terms.Max subtraction: Subtracting the row maximum before exponentiation so no exponent overflows, without changing the softmax result.
key_terms.Row reduction: A maximum or sum computed across one row, which threads of a block or warp must combine.
key_terms.Overflow: A value that exceeds the largest representable floating-point number and becomes infinity.

mistake: replacing the expression with a mathematically equivalent floating-point formula always preserves stability.
mechanism: Softmax converts a row of logits into nonnegative weights that sum to one. Exponentiating large logits directly can overflow even when the final probabilities are ordinary finite values. Subtracting the row maximum preserves the exact mathematical ratios while keeping the largest exponential at one. A kernel needs a maximum reduction, exponentials, a sum reduction and division, with correct row boundaries and accumulation precision. Define behavior for masks and exceptional inputs separately; an all-masked row cannot be treated as an ordinary finite row without a policy. Test short, ragged and extreme-valued rows.
example1: For logits \([1000,1001]\), subtract maximum 1001 to obtain \([-1,0]\). Exponentials are approximately \([0.367879,1]\), giving probabilities \([0.268941,0.731059]\). Directly computing \(e^{1001}\) can overflow in common floating types although the normalized answer is well behaved.
example2: For \([4,4,4]\), subtracting four produces three zeros, so each probability is one third. For a single finite logit, the output is one. These cases check normalization and row handling independently of large exponentials.

import math


def softmax(values):
    maximum = max(values)
    exp = [math.exp(v - maximum) for v in values]
    return [v / sum(exp) for v in exp]

title: Normalization, fusion and memory traffic

key_terms.Layer normalization: Rescaling each row to zero mean and unit variance, then applying learned scale and shift.
key_terms.RMS normalization: Rescaling each row by its root mean square without subtracting the mean.
key_terms.Kernel fusion: Combining steps into one kernel so intermediate values stay on chip instead of round-tripping through global memory.
key_terms.Epsilon: A small constant added to a variance or mean square so normalization never divides by zero.

It can also increase registers, complicate reuse or prevent a good library path. Specify accumulation and output types, normalization axes and learned scale/bias if present. key_terms.Scaled dot-product attention: The operation that divides query-key dot products by the square root of the key width, applies softmax and uses the resulting weights to average the values.
key_terms.Online softmax: Computing softmax over tiles while updating a running maximum and denominator, so the full score row is never stored.
key_terms.Attention mask: A rule that excludes key positions, such as future tokens in causal attention, before normalization.
key_terms.Quadratic memory: Memory that grows with sequence length squared when the full score matrix is materialized.

key_terms.memcpy_async: A cooperative copy from global to shared memory that can proceed while threads do other work.
key_terms.cuda::pipeline: A libcu++ object that tracks stages of asynchronous copies through acquire, commit, wait and release.

Double buffering alternates two storage slots but does not remove these dependencies. Hardware-accelerated paths and fallback behavior must be checked for the exact toolchain and device. Correct tail loading and barrier participation remain essential even when the happy path overlaps efficiently.

key_terms.Thread block cluster: A group of blocks scheduled together on nearby SMs, available on compute capability 9.0 and later.
key_terms.Distributed shared memory: Access by one block in a cluster to the shared memory of another block in the same cluster.
key_terms.Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA): A hardware unit that copies multidimensional tiles described by a tensor map descriptor.

TMA transfers use descriptors and completion protocols; they are not ordinary memcpy calls with a new name. Different instructions can require architecture-specific targets beyond a broad compute-capability family. Maintain a feature table for the exact operation, compiler and GPU, and retain a portable fallback. Learning the ownership diagram is useful without executing architecture-specific code.
example1: A cluster-assisted histogram can combine partial bins across cooperating blocks before global output. Before a remote shared-memory read, the producing block's storage must be initialized and remain alive through the required cluster synchronization. A block exiting early can invalidate the assumed lifetime.
example2: A feature table might mark baseline kernels available, cluster launch unavailable and a TMA experiment unqualified. Dispatch should choose the baseline, not attempt an unsupported instruction and silently label a CPU calculation as the specialized result. Feature detection is per operation, not a marketing-name comparison.
code:
capabilities = {"baseline": True, "cluster_histogram": False, "TMA_qualified": False}
selected = "cluster_histogram" if capabilities["cluster_histogram"] else "baseline"
assert selected == "baseline"
print({"selected_implementation": selected, "specialized_execution_verified": False})

tasks.question: List fields for an architecture-specific capability record.
tasks.answer: Operation, exact target requirement, device properties, compiler/library versions, launch constraints and actual execution evidence.

tasks.question: Why does a higher-looking GPU name not prove every instruction is supported?
tasks.answer: Feature families and architecture-specific variants have distinct contracts; names are not an executable compatibility check.

tasks.question: What should an unavailable cluster feature do to reading progress?
tasks.answer: Nothing. The learner can complete the model and worksheet while the optional hardware evidence remains unavailable.

tasks.question: Design a fallback histogram interface.
tasks.answer: Preserve input/bin/output semantics and return the same validated counts, while recording which implementation ran and comparing performance only within supported conditions.

reasoning.approach: Each block writes partial histogram bins to its shared memory, the cluster synchronizes, then blocks read remote bins and merge them before one global write.
reasoning.why: The cluster barrier guarantees the producer's bins are written and its shared storage still exists when a neighbor reads it.
reasoning.wrong: Reading a neighbor's distributed shared memory before the cluster sync, or after the producer block exits, reads uninitialized or freed storage.
reasoning.verify: Compare merged bins against a host histogram of the same input, and run on supported hardware only; otherwise record the check as unavailable.

reasoning.approach: Consult the capability table and dispatch to the baseline kernel when cluster launch and TMA are not qualified.
reasoning.why: The baseline computes the same counts on any supported device, so choosing it keeps results correct.
reasoning.wrong: Trying the cluster instruction and catching a failure, then labeling a CPU result as the cluster path, misreports what ran.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts selected == 'baseline' and prints specialized_execution_verified False.

reasoning.approach: Record operation, exact target requirement, device properties, compiler and library versions, launch limits and execution evidence.
reasoning.why: Each field narrows whether the feature actually applies to this device and build.
reasoning.wrong: Recording only the GPU model name omits the compiler target and launch evidence that decide support.
reasoning.verify: Have a second person reproduce dispatch from the record alone.

reasoning.approach: Check the specific feature and compile target rather than inferring support from the product name.
reasoning.why: Architecture-specific instructions belong to particular families and suffixed targets, not to every newer-sounding device.
reasoning.wrong: Assuming a larger model number includes every earlier specialized instruction can produce code the device cannot load.
reasoning.verify: Query compute capability and test the compiled target with a small probe kernel.

reasoning.approach: Leave reading progress unaffected and mark only the optional hardware evidence unavailable.
reasoning.why: The lesson's model and worksheet do not depend on cluster hardware.
reasoning.wrong: Blocking completion until a cluster-capable GPU appears punishes learners for hardware they cannot control.
reasoning.verify: Complete the lesson on a CPU-only machine and confirm progress records it.

reasoning.approach: Keep the same input, bin edges and output layout for both implementations, and log which one ran.
reasoning.why: Callers then get identical validated counts whichever path dispatch chooses.
reasoning.wrong: Letting the fallback use different bin boundaries makes outputs differ silently between devices.
reasoning.verify: Run both paths on the same input where supported and compare every bin.

title: CUTLASS, CuTe and tile abstractions
theory: layout composition, tile shapes, operation atoms, epilogues and policy choices. Compare a clear educational GEMM with a library-based specialized implementation. Introduce C++ templates gradually and connect to Python CuTe DSL work in the companion branch.
evidence: correct layouts, supported feature declaration and benchmark against an appropriate library baseline.
outcome: Configure a CUTLASS or CuTe kernel with correct layouts and benchmark it against a library baseline.

key_terms.CUTLASS: An NVIDIA C++ template library for building high-performance matrix multiply and related kernels.
key_terms.CuTe layout: A pair of shape and stride that maps logical coordinates to memory offsets in CUTLASS 3.
key_terms.Epilogue: The final stage of a GEMM kernel that applies scaling, bias or activation before storing results.
key_terms.MMA atom: The smallest matrix-multiply-accumulate instruction shape that CuTe composes into larger tiles.

mistake: a template library removes the need to understand layout or architecture support. , .
mechanism: CUTLASS supplies composable matrix-operation building blocks, while CuTe provides abstractions for shapes, strides and layout composition used in tiled algorithms. An operation atom describes a small supported operation; larger tiles organize repeated work and data movement. Epilogues transform accumulated results, often adding scale, bias or activation. Templates encode choices at compile time, but they do not absolve the programmer from understanding coordinates, alignment, resource costs and architecture support. Pin dependencies and begin with a prepared supported example. A novel tile DSL is an elective comparison, not a universal prerequisite for basic CUDA.
example1: A 2-by-3 logical tile with strides (3,1) maps coordinate (1,2) to offset five. A transposed view uses shape (3,2) and strides (1,3), mapping (2,1) to the same offset. Trace tiny layouts before interpreting a large template type.
example2: An epilogue applies bias then ReLU to accumulated values \([-2,1,4]\) with bias one, producing \([0,2,5]\). Moving the bias after ReLU would produce \([1,2,5]\), changing semantics. A fused epilogue must match the reference order, type conversion and scaling contract.
code:
assert 1 * 3 + 2 == 5
assert 2 * 1 + 1 * 3 == 5
values = [-2, 1, 4]
correct = [max(0, x + 1) for x in values]
wrong = [max(0, x) + 1 for x in values]
assert correct == [0, 2, 5] and wrong == [1, 2, 5]
print({"correct_epilogue": correct, "changed_operation_order": wrong})

tasks.question: Compute offset (1,1) under shape (2,3), strides (3,1).
tasks.answer: Four. Shape controls valid coordinates; strides control physical mapping.

tasks.question: A template instantiation compiles but fails on the target device. What is missing?
tasks.answer: Runtime architecture and operation qualification, plus correct layout/alignment and library support. Compilation alone is not dispatch evidence.

tasks.question: How should a non-tile-aligned matrix be handled?
tasks.answer: Use a supported tail strategy or reject unsupported shapes explicitly; do not assume padded storage contains valid zeros.

tasks.question: When would you choose a library epilogue over a custom kernel?
tasks.answer: When it expresses the required semantics and passes accuracy/performance tests while reducing maintenance; compare against the relevant library baseline first.

reasoning.approach: Compute offset as row times stride 3 plus column times stride 1 for the 2-by-3 tile, then apply the transposed view's strides (1, 3).
reasoning.why: Coordinate (1, 2) gives 3 + 2 = 5, and the transposed (2, 1) gives 2 + 3 = 5, so both name the same element.
reasoning.wrong: Swapping shape without swapping strides makes the transposed view index the wrong memory entirely.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts 1 * 3 + 2 == 5 and 2 * 1 + 1 * 3 == 5.

reasoning.approach: Add bias 1 to accumulators [-2, 1, 4] for [-1, 2, 5], then apply ReLU.
reasoning.why: ReLU gives [0, 2, 5], matching the reference order of operations.
reasoning.wrong: Applying ReLU first and adding bias afterward gives [1, 2, 5], which changes the first element.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts correct == [0, 2, 5] and wrong == [1, 2, 5].

reasoning.approach: Multiply row 1 by stride 3 and add column 1 times stride 1.
reasoning.why: The offset is 3 + 1 = 4, within the six-element tile.
reasoning.wrong: Using shape (2, 3) as strides gives 1 * 2 + 1 * 3 = 5, the wrong element.
reasoning.verify: Enumerate all six coordinates and confirm offsets 0 through 5 appear once.

reasoning.approach: Check that the target architecture, operation, layout and alignment are supported at runtime.
reasoning.why: Templates compile for configurations the device or library may not run.
reasoning.wrong: Treating a clean compile as proof of support ignores runtime dispatch requirements.
reasoning.verify: Run a small instantiation on the target and compare output with a reference GEMM.

reasoning.approach: Use the library's tail handling or reject shapes it does not support.
reasoning.why: Padded storage outside the logical matrix may contain arbitrary values.
reasoning.wrong: Assuming the padding is zero adds garbage into partial tiles.
reasoning.verify: Test a 5-by-7 matrix against a host reference.

reasoning.approach: Pick the library epilogue if it expresses the needed operation order and passes accuracy and speed tests.
reasoning.why: It reduces custom code to maintain.
reasoning.wrong: Writing a custom kernel before checking the library duplicates tested work.
reasoning.verify: Compare both against a reference and a library baseline.

title: PTX, SASS, JIT and inspecting generated code
theory: virtual versus hardware instruction sets, compiler resource reports, fat binaries, architecture targets, disassembly and JIT startup. Teach inspection before inline assembly. Include a short optional runtime/driver API and NVRTC comparison with fixed reviewed source paths.
evidence: explain a selected instruction sequence and validate any optimization with the existing tests.
outcome: Inspect generated PTX and SASS to explain a selected instruction sequence and validate any change with existing tests.

key_terms.PTX: The virtual instruction set that `nvcc` emits before architecture-specific assembly.
key_terms.SASS: The native machine instructions that a specific GPU architecture actually executes.
key_terms.cuobjdump: A tool that extracts embedded PTX and SASS from compiled binaries.
key_terms.Resource usage report: Compiler output from `-Xptxas -v` that lists registers, shared memory and spill bytes per kernel.

mistake: PTX instruction count equals executed hardware instruction count or fewer instructions always means faster. , .
mechanism: PTX is a virtual instruction language, while SASS describes machine instructions for a particular GPU architecture. The driver or toolchain can translate PTX differently across targets and versions. A fat binary can contain native device images and PTX fallback according to a deliberate policy. JIT can introduce cold-start cost and compatibility constraints. Inspect compiler resource reports and generated code to test a hypothesis, such as unexpected local-memory traffic, before attempting inline assembly. Counting PTX instructions does not directly count executed hardware operations or predict runtime.
example1: A high-level multiply-plus-add may become a fused instruction depending on types, options and target. If generated code changes, retain the numerical test because one rounding differs from two. A shorter instruction sequence is useful evidence only in combination with the workload's actual behavior.
example2: A per-thread array causes reported local-memory traffic. Reducing its live range may remove spills, but it can also add recomputation. Compare the compiler report, output and uninstrumented timing under the same target. Do not edit assembly until the source-level cause is understood.
code:
artifacts = {
    "source.cu": "CUDA C++ source",
    "kernel.ptx": "virtual instructions",
    "kernel.cubin": "target machine code",
    "main": "host executable",
}
assert artifacts["kernel.ptx"] != artifacts["kernel.cubin"]
print(artifacts)

tasks.question: Distinguish native image compatibility from PTX JIT compatibility.
tasks.answer: A native image targets a hardware family; PTX requires a driver/toolchain path able to understand and compile that virtual version for the device.

tasks.question: Why is PTX instruction count not a timing oracle?
tasks.answer: Translation, instruction latency, memory behavior, parallel scheduling and repeated execution all intervene.

tasks.question: What should an unsupported target diagnostic change?
tasks.answer: Revisit the supported architecture policy and toolchain, preserving a valid fallback; do not guess an architecture flag until the error disappears.

tasks.question: Design a cold-start experiment.
tasks.answer: Measure first load/JIT separately from warmed execution with source/target/driver identities and unchanged correctness fixtures.

expected_output: {'source.cu': 'CUDA C++ source', 'kernel.ptx': 'virtual instructions', 'kernel.cubin': 'target machine code', 'main': 'host executable'}

reasoning.approach: Inspect generated code to see whether multiply and add became one fused instruction, and keep the numerical test either way.
reasoning.why: A fused multiply-add rounds once instead of twice, so results can differ slightly from separate operations.
reasoning.wrong: Accepting a shorter instruction sequence as automatically better skips checking that its rounding still meets the tolerance.
reasoning.verify: Compare outputs from fused and unfused builds against a high-precision reference within a stated tolerance.

reasoning.approach: Read the compiler's local-memory report, shorten the array's live range, and rebuild for the same target.
reasoning.why: Fewer live values can remove spills, though recomputation may add instructions.
reasoning.wrong: Hand-editing SASS to remove spills makes code that cannot be rebuilt or maintained.
reasoning.verify: Compare the spill report, outputs and uninstrumented timings before and after.

reasoning.approach: Separate native cubin compatibility with a hardware family from PTX that the driver JIT-compiles.
reasoning.why: A cubin runs only on matching hardware, while PTX needs a driver that understands its virtual version.
reasoning.wrong: Assuming any PTX runs on any driver ignores version requirements.
reasoning.verify: Check the embedded targets with cuobjdump and the installed driver version.

reasoning.approach: Measure time directly rather than counting PTX instructions.
reasoning.why: Translation to SASS, latency, memory stalls and scheduling all change real cost.
reasoning.wrong: Ranking kernels by PTX length can pick a slower kernel with more memory stalls.
reasoning.verify: Time both kernels under the same conditions and compare.

reasoning.approach: Revisit the supported architecture list and toolchain, and keep a fallback.
reasoning.why: The diagnostic means the target is not supported by this build.
reasoning.wrong: Trying architecture flags until the error disappears can produce code for the wrong device.
reasoning.verify: Rebuild with the documented targets and confirm the probe kernel runs.

reasoning.approach: Time the first load including JIT separately from later warmed runs, recording source, target and driver.
reasoning.why: Cold start includes compilation and module loading that warmed runs skip.
reasoning.wrong: Averaging the first run with later runs hides the startup cost.
reasoning.verify: Run fresh processes repeatedly and compare first-run times.

title: Multiple GPUs, topology and collective communication
theory: device selection, separate contexts/address spaces, peer access, PCIe/NVLink topology, decomposition, halo exchange, collectives and failure propagation. Teach NCCL collective ordering and the distinction between more devices and efficient scaling.
evidence: correct combined result, observed topology, collective completion and strong/weak scaling interpretation where meaningful.
outcome: Verify a multi-GPU all-reduce result, record the observed topology and interpret strong or weak scaling.

key_terms.All-reduce: A collective that combines values from every participant and returns the same result to all of them.
key_terms.NCCL communicator: An object that describes the participating GPUs and their ranks for NCCL collectives.
key_terms.Peer access: The ability of one GPU to read or write another GPU's memory directly over NVLink or PCIe.
key_terms.Strong scaling: Speedup for a fixed total problem size as the number of GPUs grows.
key_terms.Weak scaling: Efficiency when the problem size grows in proportion to the number of GPUs.

mistake: two GPUs share memory automatically or multi-GPU execution proves multi-node readiness. , .
mechanism: Multiple GPUs have distinct allocations, execution contexts and communication paths. Peer access may be available for a pair, but it must be supported and explicitly configured under the platform's rules. Topology affects whether traffic uses PCIe, NVLink or other paths. A collective such as all-reduce combines values and makes the result available to every participant. Participants must agree on communicator, datatype, count and collective order; mismatches can hang or fail. Multi-GPU within one machine does not prove multi-node operation, which adds network, process-launch and failure concerns.
example1: Split \([1,2,3,4,5]\) across two devices as \([1,2,3]\) and \([4,5]\). Local sums are six and nine; a combined sum is fifteen. A gather gives the final result to one destination, whereas all-reduce gives fifteen to both participants. A CPU partition model demonstrates semantics only.
example2: For a radius-one stencil split into left and right partitions, each side needs its neighbor's boundary value before updating edge cells. Exchange halos and establish completion before reading them. Copying only the interior or assuming all device pointers share one pool breaks the contract.
code:
values = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
partials = [sum(values[:3]), sum(values[3:])]
all_reduce_model = [sum(partials)] * 2
assert partials == [6, 9] and all_reduce_model == [15, 15]
print({"CPU_collective_model": all_reduce_model, "multi_GPU_executed": False})

tasks.question: Compute strong-scaling efficiency for speedup 1.6 on two GPUs.
tasks.answer: Efficiency is \(\frac{1.6}{2}=0.8\), or 80%, for the same total problem size and timing scope.

tasks.question: Rank zero calls all-reduce while rank one calls broadcast first. Diagnose it.
tasks.answer: Collective ordering and signatures disagree; correct the shared protocol rather than adding arbitrary sleeps.

tasks.question: What can one GPU prove about two-device peer access?
tasks.answer: Nothing directly. It can validate local arithmetic and models, while peer execution remains unavailable.

tasks.question: Define weak versus strong scaling.
tasks.answer: Strong scaling fixes total work while adding devices; weak scaling grows total work with device count while keeping work per device roughly fixed.

reasoning.approach: Split [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] into [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5], sum each locally, then combine.
reasoning.why: Local sums 6 and 9 add to 15, and all-reduce delivers 15 to both devices.
reasoning.wrong: Using a gather when every device needs the total leaves the second device without the result.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts partials == [6, 9] and all_reduce_model == [15, 15], and prints multi_GPU_executed False.

reasoning.approach: Exchange one boundary value each way before updating edge cells, and wait for the exchange to complete.
reasoning.why: A radius-one stencil at the partition edge needs the neighbor's adjacent value.
reasoning.wrong: Updating edges before halos arrive uses stale or missing neighbor values.
reasoning.verify: Compare the split result against a single-array stencil on the same input.

reasoning.approach: Divide speedup 1.6 by device count 2.
reasoning.why: Efficiency is 0.8, or 80 percent, for fixed total work.
reasoning.wrong: Comparing runs with different problem sizes makes the ratio meaningless for strong scaling.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts 1.6 / 2 == 0.8.

reasoning.approach: Make every rank call the same collectives in the same order with matching arguments.
reasoning.why: Collectives pair calls across ranks by order.
reasoning.wrong: Adding sleeps does not fix mismatched collectives and can still hang.
reasoning.verify: Log each rank's call sequence and confirm they match.

reasoning.approach: Validate local arithmetic and the collective model, and mark peer execution unavailable.
reasoning.why: Peer access requires two devices and a link between them.
reasoning.wrong: Claiming peer behavior from one GPU reports evidence that was never collected.
reasoning.verify: Check the output records multi-GPU execution as unavailable.

reasoning.approach: Fix total work for strong scaling and fix work per device for weak scaling.
reasoning.why: These answer different questions about adding devices.
reasoning.wrong: Reporting weak-scaling results as strong-scaling speedup overstates gains.
reasoning.verify: Label each experiment's total and per-device problem sizes.

title: From one pad to a maintainable CUDA project
theory: `.cu` versus host `.cpp` translation units, headers, separable compilation, device linking, CMake targets, architecture lists, dependencies, tests and installable artifacts. Distinguish user-facing application paths from compiler outputs. Explain compiler/runtime/driver compatibility without adding arbitrary flags to lesson metadata.
evidence: a clean reproducible build and actual runtime tests on a declared target.
outcome: Build a CMake CUDA project cleanly from source and pass its runtime tests on a declared target architecture.

key_terms.CMake target: A named library or executable with its own sources, properties and dependencies.
key_terms.CUDA_ARCHITECTURES: A CMake property that lists the GPU architectures to generate device code for.
key_terms.Separable compilation: Compiling device code in separate translation units so kernels can call device functions defined elsewhere.
key_terms.Device linking: A link step that resolves device symbols across separately compiled objects.

mistake: a Makefile or CMake project can simply be pasted into the existing single-source pad.
mechanism: A maintainable CUDA project separates interfaces, host orchestration and device implementation without hiding ownership. Host .cpp files compile as ordinary C++; .cu files contain CUDA compilation units; headers declare shared interfaces. Calls across device translation units can require separable compilation and device linking. CMake targets should state languages, dependencies and architecture policy explicitly. A project directory cannot be pasted into a single-source coding pad. Keep external project commands in an owned scratch directory with clear source and build paths, and validate both a clean build and actual execution on supported hardware.
example1: A three-file design has include/transform.hpp declaring a host launch function, src/transform.cu defining its kernel and launch wrapper, and src/main.cpp building fixtures and validating output. The caller sees an ordinary host interface, while the implementation owns its CUDA dependencies.
example2: An undefined host launch function usually means its object was not linked or its declaration/definition disagree. An unresolved device function in another .cu file concerns device compilation/linking. These failures occur before mathematical validation and require different build fixes.
code:
project = {
    "include/transform.hpp": "host interface",
    "src/transform.cu": "kernel and launcher",
    "src/main.cpp": "fixture and validation",
    "build/": "generated artifacts",
}
assert len(project) == 4
print(project)

tasks.question: Name source and build directories in a clean out-of-source project.
tasks.answer: Keep authored files in the project root/src/include and generated files under a separate build directory; never confuse generated binaries with maintained source.

tasks.question: Why should architecture targets not come from lesson metadata argv?
tasks.answer: Build flags are reviewed execution policy, not arbitrary learner-controlled manifest commands. A prepared project can document its own deliberate external build configuration.

tasks.question: What does a successful CMake configure prove?
tasks.answer: Configuration generation only. Compilation, linking and runtime tests remain separate steps.

tasks.question: Design a project test split.
tasks.answer: Keep CPU reference/unit tests, CUDA compile checks and actual device numerical/sanitizer tests distinct with explicit unavailable reasons.

expected_output: {'include/transform.hpp': 'host interface', 'src/transform.cu': 'kernel and launcher', 'src/main.cpp': 'fixture and validation', 'build/': 'generated artifacts'}

reasoning.approach: Declare the host launch function in include/transform.hpp, define kernel and launcher in src/transform.cu, and validate fixtures in src/main.cpp.
reasoning.why: main.cpp sees only an ordinary host function, so it compiles with a host compiler and never touches kernel syntax.
reasoning.wrong: Putting the kernel declaration with triple-angle launch syntax in the header forces every includer to be compiled by nvcc.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts the four-entry project layout; also build and confirm main.cpp compiles as plain C++.

reasoning.approach: Check that the object defining the launcher is linked and that declaration and definition signatures match.
reasoning.why: An undefined host symbol is a link problem, separate from device-code linking errors.
reasoning.wrong: Rewriting kernel math to fix a link error changes code that was never the cause.
reasoning.verify: Run the linker with verbose output and confirm the symbol resolves.

reasoning.approach: Keep sources in src and include, and put generated files in a separate build directory.
reasoning.why: Separating them prevents committing or editing generated binaries.
reasoning.wrong: Building in the source tree mixes artifacts with maintained files.
reasoning.verify: Delete the build directory and confirm a clean rebuild works.

reasoning.approach: Set architecture targets in the reviewed build configuration, not from lesson metadata arguments.
reasoning.why: Build flags are execution policy that should be reviewed.
reasoning.wrong: Accepting flags from learner-controlled manifests lets arbitrary commands into builds.
reasoning.verify: Confirm the build ignores architecture flags supplied in metadata.

reasoning.approach: Treat a successful configure as proof that generation worked, then run build and tests.
reasoning.why: Configuring does not compile or link anything.
reasoning.wrong: Calling the project working after configure skips compile errors.
reasoning.verify: Run the build and tests after configure and check each status.

reasoning.approach: Separate CPU reference tests, CUDA compile checks and device numerical and sanitizer tests.
reasoning.why: Each runs in different environments with different requirements.
reasoning.wrong: Combining them means a missing GPU fails every test.
reasoning.verify: Run on a CPU-only machine and confirm device tests report unavailable.

title: Portability, operations and the cost of a GPU dependency
theory: feature detection, compatible driver/toolkit/library combinations, binary targets, runtime fallbacks, architecture-specific code, memory budgets, warm-up, diagnostics and fault reporting. Describe MIG/MPS, device sharing and GPU resets as operator-governed topics, not learner-controlled shortcuts. Explain that container boundaries do not guarantee safe isolation of arbitrary GPU code.
evidence: a deployment checklist tied to supported evidence tiers and graceful failures.
outcome: Write a deployment checklist tied to evidence tiers that fails gracefully when no supported GPU is present.

key_terms.Capability detection: Querying device count, compute capability and driver version before selecting a code path.
key_terms.Graceful failure: Stopping with a clear message and a nonzero exit instead of crashing or silently producing wrong output.
key_terms.Driver compatibility: Whether the installed driver supports the CUDA runtime version and device code that the binary contains.
key_terms.Evidence tier: A labeled level of proof, such as compiled, executed on a GPU or benchmarked, attached to a claim.

mistake: one container tag makes every NVIDIA device and driver equivalent.
mechanism: Portability means defining what is supported and how unsupported situations behave. CUDA execution requires a supported NVIDIA device and host software path; a CPU-only classroom can still teach algorithms and validate CPU references. AMD, Intel and Apple GPU programming use different backends and APIs, not an automatic CUDA compatibility promise. Detect capability for the operation, not simply the operating-system name. Containers package user-space dependencies but share host driver and hardware constraints. MIG, MPS, device sharing and resets are operator-managed topics. A teaching worker must never silently reset a shared device or erase learner state to recover from a fault.
example1: A dispatch policy offers CPU reference on every ordinary classroom and CUDA execution only after visibility, allocation and a small numerical probe succeed. It records which path actually ran. The same expected mathematical result does not make CPU output evidence of CUDA execution.
example2: A model fits on one 24 GiB GPU but fails on an 8 GiB device. The container tag is identical; the resource contract is not. Reduce the bounded workload or choose a supported alternate path, preserving the original memory error and learner source.
code:
capability = {"reading": True, "CPU_reference": True, "CUDA_device_probe": False}
selected = "CUDA" if capability["CUDA_device_probe"] else "CPU_reference"
assert selected == "CPU_reference"
print({"selected_path": selected, "CUDA_execution": "unavailable"})

tasks.question: Write a supported-surface table for Linux, WSL 2 and Mac learners.
tasks.answer: Reading/CPU references remain available across the Docker classroom. NVIDIA execution needs a separately supported Linux or WSL path and hardware; Mac local CUDA is not promised.

tasks.question: Why is an operating-system check insufficient for dispatch?
tasks.answer: Device presence, driver compatibility, feature support and memory vary independently of the OS.

tasks.question: What should a device fault preserve?
tasks.answer: Source, diagnostics, completed prior results and progress. Report unavailable execution without resetting unrelated hardware or volumes.

tasks.question: Design an optional alternate GPU backend lesson.
tasks.answer: Keep its own API/runtime/capability labels and numerical oracle, teach conceptual correspondence, and do not present it as executing CUDA kernels.

reasoning.approach: Offer the CPU reference everywhere, and enable CUDA only after device visibility, allocation and a small numerical probe all succeed.
reasoning.why: The probe checks that the device actually computes correctly, and logging the chosen path records what really ran.
reasoning.wrong: Reporting the CUDA path because the expected numbers matched hides that the CPU reference produced them.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts selected == 'CPU_reference' when the probe is False and prints CUDA_execution unavailable.

reasoning.approach: Check the model's memory need against device memory and shrink the workload or choose another path.
reasoning.why: A model fitting 24 GiB does not fit 8 GiB regardless of container tag.
reasoning.wrong: Assuming the same image guarantees the same resources hides the memory limit.
reasoning.verify: Run on the smaller device and confirm the original memory error is preserved and reported.

reasoning.approach: List reading and CPU references as available everywhere, and NVIDIA execution only on supported Linux or WSL with hardware.
reasoning.why: Mac machines lack local CUDA support.
reasoning.wrong: Promising Mac CUDA execution sets expectations the platform cannot meet.
reasoning.verify: Check each row against the documented support matrix.

reasoning.approach: Probe device presence, driver, features and memory directly.
reasoning.why: These vary independently of the operating system.
reasoning.wrong: Dispatching on OS name alone selects CUDA on Linux machines without GPUs.
reasoning.verify: Run dispatch on a GPU-less Linux machine and confirm CPU is chosen.

reasoning.approach: Keep source, diagnostics, prior results and progress, and report execution unavailable.
reasoning.why: Learners should not lose work because of a device fault.
reasoning.wrong: Resetting hardware or volumes destroys unrelated state.
reasoning.verify: Simulate a fault and confirm earlier results remain.

reasoning.approach: Label the alternate backend's API, runtime and capabilities separately, with its own numerical oracle.
reasoning.why: Conceptual correspondence teaches ideas without claiming equivalence.
reasoning.wrong: Presenting it as running CUDA kernels misleads learners.
reasoning.verify: Check labels in output name the actual backend.

title: Capstone: a measured scientific or data application
theory: requirements, numerical specification, correctness oracle, resource budget, profile-guided optimization and communication of tradeoffs.
evidence: CPU baseline, adversarial tests, sanitizer results where applicable, profiling artifacts, reproducible benchmark, failure behavior and a report stating when CPU is preferable.
outcome: Deliver a measured scientific application with a CPU baseline, adversarial tests, profiling artifacts and a reproducible benchmark.

key_terms.Research question: The specific, measurable question that the application and its benchmark are designed to answer.
key_terms.Reproducible benchmark: A measurement that another person can rerun from recorded code, inputs, environment and procedure.
key_terms.Profiling artifact: A saved profiler report or timeline that supports a stated performance claim.
key_terms.CPU preference boundary: The problem size or condition below which the CPU version is the better choice.

mistake: a performance demo without documented assumptions is a deliverable someone else can maintain.
mechanism: An independent numerical project begins with a bounded question, not a performance claim. Specify accepted input, output semantics, precision, resource budget and failure behavior. Build an independent CPU reference and adversarial fixtures before optimizing. Choose algorithms or libraries that fit the contract, then profile the complete pipeline. Retain evidence that another learner can reproduce: source, generation parameters, correctness comparisons, tool diagnostics where available and timing samples. A CPU-only project remains a valid algorithm/design portfolio piece when it clearly leaves GPU performance unmeasured.
example1: Project A filters a synthetic signal with a fixed-zero stencil, computes an energy sum and returns both transformed values and the scalar. For \([2,4,8]\), the stencil reference is \([2,\frac{14}{3},4]\). The energy is the sum of squares, \(\frac{376}{9}\). Explicitly define whether energy is computed before or after filtering.
example2: Project B aggregates graph neighbors using CSR then normalizes nonempty rows. It includes isolated nodes, duplicate-edge policy and skewed row lengths. The project can choose a library sparse multiply or a custom kernel, but must compare identical semantics and include conversion costs when the graph arrives in another format.
code:
from fractions import Fraction

filtered = [Fraction(2), Fraction(14, 3), Fraction(4)]
energy = sum(x * x for x in filtered)
assert energy == Fraction(376, 9)
print({"exact_filtered": [str(x) for x in filtered], "post_filter_energy": str(energy)})

tasks.question: Write a minimal acceptance contract for Project A.
tasks.answer: Fixed boundary policy, input dtype/length range, full filtered output, post-filter energy, error budget, memory bound and empty-input behavior.

tasks.question: A project claims a speedup but omits graph conversion. Diagnose it.
tasks.answer: If conversion is required per request, include it. If reused, state and measure the reuse contract explicitly.

tasks.question: Give three adversarial fixtures.
tasks.answer: Empty input, a singleton/boundary case and a ragged or skewed case; add extreme numeric values when the operation permits them.

tasks.question: Decide whether the GPU earns deployment.
tasks.answer: Compare end-to-end benefit, accuracy, setup/maintenance cost and supported hardware. Keeping a CPU implementation can be the evidence-based result.

reasoning.approach: Apply the fixed-zero stencil to [2, 4, 8], then square and sum the filtered values with exact fractions.
reasoning.why: The middle value averages 2, 4 and 8 to 14/3, and edges average with zero, giving energy 376/9.
reasoning.wrong: Computing energy on the unfiltered signal returns 84, a different quantity than the contract asks for.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts energy == Fraction(376, 9) and prints the exact filtered values.

reasoning.approach: Build CSR from edges, aggregate neighbors, then normalize only rows with nonzero degree.
reasoning.why: Isolated nodes have no neighbors, so skipping their normalization avoids dividing by zero.
reasoning.wrong: Normalizing every row divides isolated rows by zero and spreads NaN.
reasoning.verify: Include isolated nodes, duplicates and skewed rows, and compare against a host reference.

reasoning.approach: State boundary policy, dtype and length range, full output, energy, error budget, memory bound and empty behavior.
reasoning.why: Each item defines what passing means.
reasoning.wrong: Checking only the energy scalar lets filter errors cancel and pass.
reasoning.verify: Write a test for each contract item.

reasoning.approach: Include graph conversion in timing if each request needs it.
reasoning.why: Conversion cost is part of end-to-end work when repeated.
reasoning.wrong: Timing only the kernel overstates speedup.
reasoning.verify: Time conversion plus kernel and report both.

reasoning.approach: Use empty input, a singleton or boundary case, and a skewed case.
reasoning.why: These expose edge and load-balance bugs.
reasoning.wrong: Testing only typical sizes misses failures at edges.
reasoning.verify: Add extreme values when the operation allows them.

reasoning.approach: Compare end-to-end benefit, accuracy, setup and maintenance cost, and supported hardware.
reasoning.why: These decide whether the GPU path is worth it.
reasoning.wrong: Deploying because the kernel is faster ignores total cost.
reasoning.verify: Document the decision, including keeping the CPU path.

title: Capstone: a custom ML operator that earns its existence
prerequisite_note: The framework-binding part of this capstone also uses `cuda-097` (a Python API over a CUDA C++ operator) and `cuda-098` (backward as part of the operator) from the Python branch. They come later in the subject order, so read them before that part rather than treating them as a gate for opening this chapter.
theory: custom kernels versus existing framework operations, forward/backward contracts, shapes, strides, dtypes, devices, stream semantics, error propagation, packaging and regression coverage. Include framework gradcheck or a justified equivalent where differentiability is relevant.
evidence: supported-contract documentation, forward and backward tests, invalid-input behavior, end-to-end measurement and an honest decision to keep or reject the custom kernel.
outcome: Implement a custom ML operator with forward and backward tests, input validation and an end-to-end keep or reject decision.

key_terms.Forward contract: The documented shapes, dtypes, devices and layouts that an operator accepts and returns.
key_terms.Backward pass: The computation of input gradients from output gradients that training frameworks require.
key_terms.Gradient check: Comparing analytic gradients with finite-difference estimates at chosen points.
key_terms.Current stream: The framework's active CUDA stream, which a custom operator must launch on to keep ordering correct.

mistake: faster forward execution alone proves the operator improves training or is safe for arbitrary framework tensors.
mechanism: A custom ML operator has a forward contract and, when differentiable, a backward contract. State supported shape, strides, dtype, device, aliasing and stream behavior. Reject unsupported inputs before unsafe access. The operator must integrate with the framework's ownership and current-stream rules, not merely return plausible numbers. Compare against a readable framework reference and the framework's optimized or compiled path where available. Measure full training or inference scope, including backward, transfers and launch overhead. A faster forward kernel can still make training slower or produce wrong gradients.
example1: For affine \(y=ax+b\) with a=3, b=1 and x=\([-1,0,2]\), forward output is \([-2,1,7]\). If a scalar loss sums outputs, each input gradient is three. A custom forward that returns the right values but backward returns one is mathematically wrong despite passing the forward fixture.
example2: For a fused bias-plus-ReLU, derivative at a nonzero preactivation is one when positive and zero when negative, multiplied by incoming gradient. The exact zero point needs the framework's chosen convention. A finite-difference check near a kink can be misleading, so test smooth points and the explicit boundary policy separately.
code:
x, a, b = [-1.0, 0.0, 2.0], 3.0, 1.0
forward = [a * value + b for value in x]
assert forward == [-2.0, 1.0, 7.0]


def loss(values):
    return sum(a * value + b for value in values)


epsilon = 1e-5
gradients = []
for i in range(len(x)):
    plus, minus = x.copy(), x.copy()
    plus[i] += epsilon
    minus[i] -= epsilon
    gradients.append((loss(plus) - loss(minus)) / (2 * epsilon))
assert all(abs(g - a) < 1e-8 for g in gradients)
print({"forward": forward, "CPU_finite_difference_gradients": gradients})

tasks.question: Compute input gradients for loss=sum(3*x+1).
tasks.answer: Every component is three. Also test parameter gradients if a and b are learnable in the declared interface.

tasks.question: A kernel assumes contiguous tensors but accepts transposed views. Diagnose it.
tasks.answer: Either implement stride-aware indexing, make an explicit accounted copy or reject unsupported layouts; do not reinterpret shape as contiguity.

tasks.question: What should an unsupported dtype do?
tasks.answer: Raise a clear validation error before launch or select a documented fallback; never cast silently if it changes the operator contract.

tasks.question: Define final acceptance for the custom operator.
tasks.answer: Forward/reference parity, backward checks, boundary and invalid-input tests, stream/lifetime correctness, real GPU evidence when claimed and end-to-end comparison against a strong framework baseline.

reasoning.approach: Compute forward 3x + 1 on [-1, 0, 2], then check gradients of the summed loss with central finite differences.
reasoning.why: Forward gives [-2, 1, 7], and each input gradient of sum(3x + 1) is the slope 3.
reasoning.wrong: A backward pass returning 1 passes every forward test while giving wrong gradients to training.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts forward == [-2.0, 1.0, 7.0] and every finite-difference gradient within 1e-8 of 3.

reasoning.approach: Multiply the incoming gradient by 1 for positive preactivations and 0 for negative ones.
reasoning.why: ReLU's derivative is a step, so the mask selects which gradients pass.
reasoning.wrong: Finite-differencing exactly at zero straddles the kink and gives one half.
reasoning.verify: Test points away from zero numerically, and check the zero convention against the framework.

reasoning.approach: Differentiate sum(3x + 1) with respect to each x.
reasoning.why: Each derivative is 3, independent of x.
reasoning.wrong: Returning the forward values as gradients confuses outputs with derivatives.
reasoning.verify: Compare analytic gradients with the finite differences in the reference.

reasoning.approach: Use stride-aware indexing, make an explicit copy, or reject non-contiguous inputs.
reasoning.why: A transposed view has the same shape but different strides.
reasoning.wrong: Indexing as contiguous reads elements in the wrong order.
reasoning.verify: Pass a transposed tensor and compare against the reference.

reasoning.approach: Raise a validation error before launch or use a documented fallback.
reasoning.why: The operator contract defines supported dtypes.
reasoning.wrong: Silently casting can change precision and results.
reasoning.verify: Pass an unsupported dtype and assert the error.

reasoning.approach: Require forward parity, gradient checks, edge and invalid tests, stream safety, GPU evidence and baseline comparison.
reasoning.why: Together these show the operator is correct and worthwhile.
reasoning.wrong: Accepting it on speed alone ignores correctness and maintenance.
reasoning.verify: Run each check and record results before adoption.
